I drift off into a world of my own

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

vignette:
Kofi has been the head librarian at the city’s main branch for twenty-two years, a role he has always considered a sacred trust. At seventy-eight, he still moves with a quiet dignity, his posture straight, his hands gentle as they handle the books he has spent a lifetime curating. It was in a place much like his library, a university lecture hall where he was attending a talk on post-colonial literature, that his world was fractured. He remembers the afternoon light slanting through the tall windows, the low murmur of the crowd, the scent of old paper and dust. Then, the shattering of glass, the screams, and the sudden, incomprehensible violence. The attackers moved with a chilling purpose that defied all reason. What stays with Kofi is not just the fear, but the profound offense of it—the violation of a space dedicated to thought and peace. He saw people behaving not as humans, but as instruments of chaos, and that image became the seed of a perpetual dread.

In the months that followed, the memory began to unspool in his mind against his will. It is not a hazy recollection but a pristine, high-definition recording. He can still see the exact pattern on the carpet where a woman fell, the specific shade of blue of the lecturer's tie, the expression of disbelief on a young man's face. The memory plays like a film on a loop, especially at night, robbing him of sleep. During the day, it lies in wait. A car backfiring on the street outside the library, the sudden slam of a book on a table—any sharp, unexpected noise can instantly transport him back to that lecture hall, his heart pounding in his chest, the smell of cordite sharp in his nostrils. His surroundings dissolve, and for a few terrifying seconds, he is there again.

His life, once expansive, has contracted into a small, tightly controlled space. He and his wife, Adanna, used to love visiting the weekend farmer's market, but Kofi can no longer tolerate the press of bodies. He sees threats in the jostling of the crowd, potential chaos in every interaction. He has come to believe that the world is fundamentally unsafe, that the veneer of civility is thin and easily torn. Even the library, his sanctuary, has become a source of anxiety. When a group of teenagers gathers by the computer terminals, their laughter a little too loud, their disregard for the quiet a minor infraction, Kofi feels a surge of panic that is wildly disproportionate. He sees in their carelessness the same disregard for order that he witnessed in the attackers. He feels his hands tremble and must retreat to the quiet of the archives, his mind drifting into a fog, a fantasy of a quiet, orderly world that no longer seems to exist.

This retreat has become his primary coping mechanism. When Adanna tries to talk to him about the news, especially stories of conflict or injustice, he finds his mind simply checking out, floating away into a silent, grey space where nothing can touch him. He has also begun to actively push away joy. His granddaughter’s eighth birthday party was last month, and he couldn't bring himself to go. The thought of the bright balloons, the happy shouting of children, the simple celebration of life—it all felt like a lie. He was certain that allowing himself to feel that happiness would be a betrayal of those who suffered, or worse, an invitation for disaster to strike again. Adanna went alone, and the silence in the house when she returned was heavier than any argument. It was the growing distance between them, and the looming anniversary of the attack, that finally made him pick up the phone. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a quiet, desperate plea: to find a way to live in the world again without being constantly at war with his own mind.
